_comment: Neutral go->rust rule pack. Package-local mirror of the forever home
specs/port-rules/lang/go-rust/**; the engine reads only what is here.
Rule order in `rules` IS the transform order, and `precedence` must agree with it — the
loader refuses a pack where the two disagree rather than silently obeying one of them.
type_map is keyed by TYPE IDENTITY, not by spelling: a primitive by its bare name, a named
type by `package.Name`. The two cannot collide because a qualified key always carries a dot
a bare name may not. A named type this map does not carry, from a unit the corpus also
translates, resolves through that unit's emitted module instead — which is the case a
spelling table could not express at all.
type_constructors answers for a COMPOSITE by its constructor rather than its shape. One
`slice` entry answers every slice; a spelling table needed a row per element type.
type_map_overrides: one source type does not always take one target type. `string` becomes
an owned String where a value is stored — a field, a parameter, a return — and CANNOT be one
in a constant, because a Rust const must be known at compile time and String is
heap-allocated. Recording that here rather than branching on it keeps the decision reviewable.
pointer_dispositions decide what a pointer BECOMES, from facts the front end observed, in
declared order with the first match winning. Go is garbage-collected, so a `*T` says nothing
about ownership; the decision has to be made and it has to be recorded. Order matters: the
two conservative rules come first, so an escaping or unanalysed pointer never reaches a
borrow rule. There is deliberately NO catch-all — facts nothing accepts refuse, because an
invented default is a decision nobody wrote down.
copy_types names the SOURCE types whose target counterpart copies, keyed by source identity
the same way type_map is, so the two tables answer for the same thing. Reading anything else
by value MOVES in the target, which does not compile out of a borrow — so the read is cloned:
`return c.label` returns a copy in the source and the receiver survives, while the same text
in Rust moves out of `&self`.
zero_values is what a struct literal's OMITTED fields become. Go fills them with the field
type's zero and the target rejects an incomplete literal, so the engine spells them out. A
type with no entry refuses by name rather than falling back to `Default::default()`, which
would compile for these four and quietly mean something else for a type whose Default is not
its zero.
trait_object_forms is how a TRAIT reaches a value position. The source holds an interface
value directly and the target cannot — a trait has no size — so it arrives as `&dyn T`,
`Box<dyn T>`, `Rc<dyn T>` or a generic parameter, and those are different answers to who owns
the value and how long it lives. Only `param` is declared: a borrow is unambiguously right
there and the caller keeps the value. `result` is deliberately absent, so returning an
interface refuses by name rather than being boxed on a guess.
The supertrait position takes the bare path: an embedded interface becomes a trait BOUND, which
is the one place a trait appears as itself rather than as something holding it. Declared rather
than special-cased in the engine, so every position answers the same way.
failure_convention is what makes a function FALLIBLE. The source returns failure as a trailing
result of a designated type, checked by convention rather than enforced; the target expresses
it as the whole return type. Only the SOURCE side is declared here — which type carries the
convention and how the absent value is spelled — because `Result`, `Ok` and `Err` are target
spellings and the face that renders the target owns them.
The target type is a boxed trait object rather than a `thiserror` enum because the emitted
crate is compiled against the standard library alone. A real port declares its own error type
here and nothing in the engine changes.
function_map answers for a CALL the way type_map answers for a type, keyed by source identity
so a local named `errors` cannot be mistaken for the package. It is not optional for a real
package: every one calls its standard library, and the standard library is exactly the part
that does not come along. `len` casts because the source's `len` returns its `int`, which this
pack maps to `i64`, and the target's returns a `usize`.
A template brackets ITSELF where it needs to. The engine substitutes text and does not know
what the surrounding expression will be, so a template whose result binds looser than a caller
might is the template author's problem to parenthesise — the same contract type_constructors has.
The type map covers the source's WHOLE basic set, because a real package uses most of it in
its first file — a map sized to a fixture corpus is a map sized to what the engine already
handled. `int` and `int64` both take `i64` because the source's `int` is 64-bit on every
platform this programme targets; `rune` is a code point and takes `char`, not `i32`, because
the target has a type for exactly that and using it keeps the meaning.
The `untyped` rows are the source's UNTYPED CONSTANTS, which carry a default type rather than
a declared one. They are listed rather than folded into their defaults because they are
distinct identities in the front end and a table that answered for one and not the other would
resolve a constant and refuse the variable beside it.
complex64/128 map to a name the target does not have, ON PURPOSE. The target has no complex
type and inventing one silently would be worse than the compile error this produces; the row
exists so the failure names the type rather than reading as an unmapped-type hole.
`error` maps to the TRAIT, not to a boxed one. Where a trait may stand is a position question
the trait_object_forms table answers, so a parameter becomes `&dyn std::error::Error` and a
result — which the target must own — refuses until the pack declares how it is owned.

trait_receiver.reason: A Go interface says nothing about how an implementation binds its receiver, and the implementations are not all in view, so this cannot be recovered from the source — it can only be decided. EXCLUSIVE is the choice that does not silently forbid something: a shared receiver makes a mutating method like Named.Rename unimplementable, whereas an exclusive one only demands mutability from implementations that do not need it, which is a compile-time inconvenience rather than a lost capability. Revisit when the front end reports per-method mutation; see docs/programs/k8s-port/census/ownership-escape.md.

deferred_kinds.reason: A package-level var is a MUTABLE global. Rust's `static` is immutable, so emitting one would silently drop the mutability the declaration exists for; `static mut` is unsafe and `OnceLock`/`Mutex` each pick a synchronization policy the source never stated. Choosing among those is a rule decision, not a default. See docs/programs/k8s-port/census/ownership-escape.md and concurrency.md.

pointer_dispositions.reason: The pointer outlives the call — it is returned or captured — so no borrow can be handed out: a reference would need a lifetime the caller cannot supply. Owned is the form that is always available, and `Option` carries the nil the source could hold. NO RECEIVER FORM: a method whose receiver escapes cannot be a borrow of self, and refusing is better than picking a borrow that will not hold.

The pointer reached a call the front end did not analyse, so 'not mutated' and 'does not escape' are UNPROVEN rather than false. A borrow chosen on unproven facts is a guess; the owned form costs a move and cannot be wrong. Revisit when the analysis follows calls.

The body provably assigns through this pointer and nothing outlives the call, so an exclusive borrow is what the code does. This is a HYPOTHESIS about aliasing, not a proof: escape analysis shows lifetime compatibility and not the exclusivity a borrow needs, because a Go caller may pass one pointer as two arguments. What makes it safe to emit is that the target checks it — an unsatisfiable `&mut` is a borrow-check error the compile proof catches, which is a red build rather than silent corruption. See docs/programs/k8s-port/census/ownership-escape.md.

Nothing mutates through it and nothing outlives the call, so a shared borrow is both sufficient and the cheapest form. Same aliasing caveat as the exclusive case, and much weaker: a shared borrow coexists with other shared borrows, so caller-side aliasing does not invalidate it.
